I disagree within specialized domains under discussion. Let's say you're hiring a network engineer to design a network infrastructure for a new building. That's a short-term gig. The job won't be there when the work is done. You need someone willing and able to work full time (possibly quitting his job) or someone who only works on gigs like this. He has expenses related to the type of work that aren't otherwise covered: He has to look for a new job when this one is over. If you're not offering a salary he can live on longer than the work contract, he won't take it.

But it goes beyond officially short-term gigs when you consider the fluid modern economy. A factory building truck beds might not be operating in three years when a new design comes out. A paper mill might close, a type of memory may be obsolete in five years. The days of taking a job with one company and staying there until you retire are long gone, with temp agencies picking up the slack in many cases.

A worker considering a career in a fluid industry would be wise to count the cost of moving and job hunting in his salary requirement. And ever-fewer industries are static enough for this to not apply. This must drive up the required compensation for that kind of work. To require the government to step in is effectively to require a subsidy.
